---
title: "Three Kinds of Machine"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will tell apart a deterministic program, a trained model and an LLM, and pick the right one for a job.
- **Before you start:** [Name the Fears](name-the-fears.html).
- **Time:** about 10 minutes.
:::

## Three kinds

- **A deterministic program** (a script, `awk`, `samtools`): the same input always gives the same output, and you can read why. Use it whenever the rule is known.
- **A trained model** (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor): learned from data to do **one task**, with measured accuracy on that task. It is the predictive side of AI: it forecasts from past data and gives you an estimate to act on. Use it when the rule is unknown but the task is narrow and validated.
- **A large language model (LLM)**: trained on large amounts of text, then tuned to follow instructions. It is the generative side of AI: it produces new content (text, code, images) that you review, flexible and fluent, with no built-in guarantee of correctness. Use it where the task is open-ended and you can check the result, such as drafting, explaining, or writing a first version of code that you then test.

The line between the last two is not clean. An LLM can be asked to classify, and some generative models predict structure or sequences. Judge a tool by the task you give it and how you will check the result. For a forecast, a simpler predictive model usually does the job more cheaply than a generative one.

Two common mistakes: using an LLM to do something a one-line script does exactly (slow, costly, and sometimes wrong), and trusting a model outside the task it was validated for.

An LLM can also be called **inside a script** (for example to tidy free-text labels). That makes your pipeline non-deterministic, so the result needs its own checks and the exact model and version recorded.

Before you reach for an agent or a large model, ask whether a script, a fixed workflow or a smaller specialised model does the job. A method that fits the task is often cheaper to run and easier to reproduce, and it does not change when a provider updates a hosted model. Keep the large model for the open-ended steps.

## Should you fine-tune? A note on LoRA

LoRA (low-rank adaptation) is a way to **fine-tune**: you freeze the model's weights and train small extra "adapter" matrices on your own examples. That needs far less memory than retraining everything, and the adapter can later be merged into the base model. It changes the model itself, so it belongs to the trained-model kind.

Consider LoRA when all of these hold:

- You have the **model weights**. An open-weight model you can download qualifies; a hosted model reached through an API usually does not.
- The task is **narrow and repeatable**: the same kind of input and output every time, such as tagging text with a fixed label set.
- You have **examples with known answers**, enough to train on and to hold some back for testing.
- You have an **eval** that shows the tuned model beats the untuned one on that task.

For agent work, a clearer prompt, better tools and a working eval usually give more return first, and they cost less to change. Fine-tune when you can show those fall short on a narrow task. Fine-tuning adds things to track: the training data, the adapter version and the base model it belongs to.

## What a model can do on its own

A language model with no tools suits some jobs and struggles with others. A large hosted model will do better than a small one on some rows.

| Suits | Struggles with |
|---|---|
| Summarising and editing text | Counting letters or basic arithmetic |
| Pulling out names and places | Multi-step logical reasoning |
| Classifying a piece of text | Facts it was never given |
| Generating tags, short creative writing | Writing code (a small on-device model) |

Harder tasks become possible once the model can call tools or produce structured output. That is the idea behind an agent: the model reads and writes, and a harness gives it tools (a shell, a file editor, a script runner) for the parts it finds hard. Counting and arithmetic are good work to hand to a script.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents): Anthropic, article. Why read: it separates fixed workflows from agents and argues for the simplest option, which is the choice this quest asks you to make.
- [AI for Science, practice 1: match the method to the task](https://aiforscience.eu/best-practices/01-match-method-to-task/): AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it argues for the cheapest method that fits, with a script or small model before an agent. It is a draft with no endorsements yet.
- [Understand model capabilities](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundationmodels/generating-content-and-performing-tasks-with-foundation-models#Understand-model-capabilities): Apple, docs. Why read: it is a short table of what a small on-device model suits and what it does not, a useful reminder of what a model can do before you give it tools.
- [Generative AI vs. predictive AI: What's the difference?](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai-vs-predictive-ai-whats-the-difference): IBM, article. Why read: a short vendor explainer of the two terms, with business examples; it is secondary and written for enterprise readers, so use it for the vocabulary.
- [Fine-tuning LLMs Guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide): Unsloth, docs. Why read: a beginner-friendly walk through LoRA, QLoRA, dataset shape and training settings; it is a vendor guide for its own tool, so treat its speed and hardware claims as the vendor's.
- [LoRA](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/main/en/conceptual_guides/lora): Hugging Face, docs. Why read: the PEFT library's explanation of how LoRA works, what rank and alpha control, and how to merge an adapter back into the base model.
- [Define success criteria and build evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows how to turn "it seems fine" into a measurable check, which is how you test an LLM step.
:::
